newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sell call for Pakistan's Hub Power Co.
newsitem.headline: Sell call for Pakistan's Hub Power Co.

text.p: Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia (CLSA) has advised clients to sell Pakistan's blue-chip Hub Power Co Ltd (Hubco) due to what it says is an increase in Hubco's risk profile.

In a research note received by Reuters on Tuesday, Credit Lyonnais said signs that the government wanted to renegotiate power purchase agreements with private power plants had clouded the realisation of returns earlier thought guaranteed.
This had raised the risk premium for all the private power companies, including Hubco.
"The government is finding it difficult to meet its financial obligations towards IPPs (independent power plants)," Credit Lyonnais said.
It said any renegotiation of power purchase tariffs would place a question mark over returns earlier guaranteed under power purchase agreements.

Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif last month told the government to set up a committee to study the power purchase agreements signed by the previous government with a view to persuading some two dozen power companies to reduce agreed tariffs.

Newspapers have quoted Hubco chief executive Mike Woodroffe as saying Hubco was prepared to sell power at lower rates by cutting costs where it could, without renegotiating the power purchase agreement.
"We are aware of ways to reduce cost without an attempt to renegotiate our agreements with the government," Woodroffe said, but added: "There is little room for cuts."
Under an agreement signed in 1993, Hubco sells electricity to the state-run Water and Power Development Authority at a rate of $0.725 per kilowatt hour (KWh).
But with higher capacity utilisation and lowering of cost the average tariff for 30 years could decline to $0.54 per KWh, Woodroffe was quoted as saying.

The former government led by Benazir Bhutto issued letters of support between 1994 and 1996 for almost 3,000 megawatt (MW) of new capacity, at a guaranteed payment of $0.65 per KWH for the first 10 years, in a bid to attract foreign investment.
Almost all these projects are expected to come on stream by the end of 1998.

"As per CLSA estimates, the capacity payments for the 3,000 MW come to around $700 million per annum. If we add payments for Hubco and Kot Addu (which was privatised last year), the total is a staggering $1.275 billion (a year)," Credit Lyonnais said.

To meet these bills, the government, already facing a foreign exchange crunch, would have to raise power rates by 33 percent. That might not only be politically suicidal but also render domestic industry non-competitive, it said.
"Amid growing signs that the government might go back on its guarantees, Hubco's required rate of return must rise to reflect the risk of a weaker sovereign guarantee," it added.
Credit Lyonnais said it had recommended investors to sell Hubco because it was now overvalued. It said the shares should be worth 30.30 rupees ($0.74) per share.
Hub Power Co fell 0.50 rupees to 37.15 rupees on Monday, but recovered 0.10 to close at 37.25 on Tuesday.
